claims.quote: The only exceptions are for certain married couples filing a joint federal return in the following situations: / One spouse is a New York State resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident. / In this case, you must either: – file separate New York returns using filing status ; or – file jointly, as if you both were New York State residents, using filing status .
claims.why_uncovered: The status item is bound to the federal filing status from IT-201 item A, and it cites only the general rule that the New York status follows the federal one. Nothing in the encoding covers the exception for a married couple filing a joint federal return where one spouse is a New York State resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident. In that case the couple must file separate New York returns (married filing separately) or file jointly as if both were residents. The encoding has no question that asks this and no refusal for it. The HANDLED ELSEWHERE refusals deal with federal filing-status tests and with nonresident aliens for the EIC. None of them covers New York residency of one spouse.

sentences.quote: Complete Form IT-2, Summary of W-2 Statements, for all federal Forms W-2 (or W-2c) you received.
Foreign income If you received foreign income but did not receive a federal Form W-2, you must complete Form IT-2.

claims.quote: Complete Form IT-2, Summary of W-2 Statements, for all federal Forms W-2 (or W-2c) you received. / Foreign income If you received foreign income but did not receive a federal Form W-2, you must complete Form IT-2.
claims.why_uncovered: Each encoded question asks for an amount 'on this Form W-2'. No question asks whether a Form W-2c corrected the original W-2, and nothing refuses that case. So the record could carry the original withholding instead of the corrected amount, and the same gap applies to the city and Yonkers withholding questions. Nothing in the encoding asks about, builds or refuses the separate IT-2 record that is required for foreign income received without a Form W-2. Every record the encoding builds starts from a Form W-2, so this required entry is never made.

claims.page: ny_it201i p. 4; ny_it201i p. 5; ny_it201i p. 6
claims.why_uncovered: The encoding takes the New York filing status from the federal return. Its only filing-status exception is ny_it201.gate.spouse_nonresident, which covers a spouse who was a nonresident or part-year resident. No question or refusal covers a joint federal filer who files a separate New York return because the spouse's whereabouts are unknown or the spouse refuses to sign. In that case the filer moves to married filing separately, which changes the standard deduction, the tax computation, the household credit tables and the item H dependent count.

sentences.quote: However, if your 2024 New York adjusted gross income was more than $150,000 (or $75,000 if you are married filing separately for 2025) and you are not a farmer or a fisherman, your 2025 prepayments must equal at least 110% of your 2024 New York income tax based on a 12-month return.

claims.quote: However, if your 2024 New York adjusted gross income was more than $150,000 (or $75,000 if you are married filing separately for 2025) and you are not a farmer or a fisherman, your 2025 prepayments must equal at least 110% of your 2024 New York income tax based on a 12-month return.
claims.why_uncovered: ny_it201.ask.prior_agi_high asks only about 2024 New York AGI. No question asks whether the filer is a farmer or fisherman, and nothing refuses that case. A farmer or fisherman with high prior-year AGI keeps the 100% safe harbor, but the encoding applies the 110% one. That can wrongly trigger the estimated-penalty gate or misstate the line 81 penalty.

claims.quote: The only exceptions are for certain married couples filing a joint federal return in the following situations: • One spouse is a New York State resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident. / In this case, you must either: – file separate New York returns using filing status ; or – file jointly, as if you both were New York State residents, using filing status .
claims.why_uncovered: The status item just uses the federal filing status from IT-201 Item A, citing only the general rule "In most cases, you must use the same filing status you used on your federal return." No question asks whether each spouse on a joint federal return was a New York resident, nonresident or part-year resident. No refusal on this form or in the HANDLED ELSEWHERE list covers this case. That list's only residency-related refusal is the federal EIC refusal for nonresident aliens, which is a different situation. So when one spouse is a New York resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident, New York requires either separate returns (filing status ③) or a joint return as if both were residents. The encoding would still take the married filing jointly schedule straight from the federal return and never offer the separate-return choice that this exception requires.
